# What PhyloTrace Is {#sec-intro}

PhyloTrace is an open-source platform for **bacterial pathogen monitoring at the
genomic level**. It takes whole-genome assemblies, types them by core-genome
multilocus sequence typing (cgMLST), screens them for antimicrobial-resistance
determinants, and enables exploration of the relationships between isolates
through interactive trees, networks, curves, maps and heatmaps — all from a
local, portable database. This chapter introduces the problem PhyloTrace
addresses, its position among related typing methods, and the workflow
documented in the rest of the manual.

## The problem {#sec-intro-problem}

When several patients carry the same pathogen, three questions typically
arise: whether the infections are related, whether they share a common
source, and whether the outbreak is ongoing. Traditional typing methods
answered these coarsely. Whole-genome sequencing answers them at the finest
possible resolution — but turning raw genomes into a defensible, comparable
answer requires a pipeline most labs cannot assemble from scratch.

::: {.callout-tip title="Concept — what PhyloTrace is for"}
PhyloTrace exists to make genomic pathogen surveillance usable without
requiring a bioinformatician. It encapsulates the computationally intensive
steps — allele typing, resistance screening, distance calculation, tree and
network building — behind a graphical interface, and stores everything in one
portable database file so that comparing isolates within a lab, or between
labs, is a matter of loading (or sharing) a file.
:::

## Where cgMLST sits {#sec-intro-cgmlst}

PhyloTrace is built on **cgMLST**. To place it:

- **Classical MLST** [@maiden1998mlst] types ~7 housekeeping genes and assigns a
  sequence type (ST). Portable and stable, but low resolution — many unrelated
  isolates share an ST. PhyloTrace still computes it, alongside cgMLST
  (@sec-typing).
- **cgMLST** extends the same allele-by-allele logic to the whole **core genome**
  (thousands of loci). It keeps MLST's portability — every lab gets the same
  allele calls against a standard scheme — while gaining the resolution to
  separate outbreak isolates from background (@sec-concepts).
- **SNP typing** compares genomes base-by-base. Highest resolution, but its
  results depend on the reference and pipeline, which makes cross-lab comparison
  harder. cgMLST trades a little resolution for standardisation and portability.

PhyloTrace downloads cgMLST schemes from **cgMLST.org** [@cgmlstorg] and resolves
the accompanying classical MLST scheme against **PubMLST** and Institut Pasteur
[@pubmlst] (@sec-typing-classical). Its allele identity by content hash aligns it
with tools such as **chewBBACA** [@silva2018chewbbaca]; its minimum spanning
trees follow the goeBURST / PHYLOViZ tradition [@francisco2009goeburst;
@nascimento2017phyloviz].

## The workflow {#sec-intro-workflow}

Everything in PhyloTrace follows one linear path, shown in @fig-preface-workflow.
The stages correspond to the chapters of this manual:

1. **Manage a scheme** — download a cgMLST scheme for the target species
   (@sec-schemes).
2. **Type assemblies** — submit FASTA files; they are typed (cgMLST and classical
   MLST) and AMR-screened, and appended to the database in real time
   (@sec-typing, @sec-amr).
3. **Build and curate the database** — browse, edit, add custom variables, delete
   (@sec-browser); import and export to collaborate (@sec-interop).
4. **Visualize** — MSTs, NJ/UPGMA trees, epi curves, maps and AMR heatmaps,
   enriched with metadata (@sec-mst through @sec-amr-heatmap).
5. **Save** — persist plots into the Analysis Dashboard, stored inside the same
   database (@sec-dashboard).

## What to read next {#sec-intro-next}

Read @sec-concepts next — it explains every method the app uses, in plain
language, and the later chapters point back to it. If you would rather start at
the app itself, @sec-app-basics describes how PhyloTrace behaves as you work in
it and @sec-data describes the database file everything revolves around; the
component chapters then follow the workflow in order.

The [References](references.qmd) collect the primary literature and
@sec-glossary defines the terms used throughout.
